            18              Conclusions




                            18.1 Summary of the book
                            18.2 Where do we go from here?



                          In this book, I have tried to provide the determined reader with a fair summary of
                          the state of our existing knowledge about exchange rates and an adequate foun-
                          dation for getting to grips with the original literature, if so desired. The concluding
                          chapter will briefly survey the material in the book, then go on to consider the
                          question: where might research go from here?


                   18.1 Summary of the book
                          In the first chapter the reader was introduced to the working of a currency market
                          under fixed and floating exchange rates and the significance of the balance of pay-
                          ments was explained. As a background to the theory to follow, a brief history of the
                          international monetary system was given, with particular emphasis on the prelude to
                          today’s floating exchange rates: the disintegration of the Bretton Woods regime and
                          the series of attempts to reimpose fixed exchange rates, culminating in the ongoing
                          experiment with currency unions.
                             There followed three chapters of essential preliminaries. In the first, it was shown
                          how extending the law of one price to product markets in the open economy led to
                          the conclusion that price levels ought to move in unison, once allowance was made
                          for exchange rate movements. Unfortunately, however attractive it might look in
                          theory, purchasing power parity turned out to fit the facts very poorly, if at all.
                             By contrast, extending the law of one price to the market for international securit-
                          ies looked more promising. Two conclusions emerged from Chapter 3. First, arbitrage
                          ought to make the forward premium equal to the international interest differential –
                          and, by and large, the evidence suggests it does. On the other hand, uncovered interest
                          rate parity is much more difficult to test since it involves the unobservable expected
                          rate of depreciation.
                             Finally in Part I, Chapter 4 extended the textbook aggregate demand and supply
                          framework to accommodate an open economy.
                             The preliminaries completed, Part II examined a number of models of exchange
                          rate determination, starting with the monetary model, a convenient benchmark for
ERA_C18.qxd 09/27/2004 03:09PM Page 476




         476 Chapter 18 · Conclusions

                         future reference. In essence it is an extension of the classical quantity theory to the
                         open economy context. First, it predicts that increases in the money stock will be
                         reflected in depreciation of the same proportion and, second, that (real) income
                         growth will be associated with a rising international currency value. Both results
                         automatically flow from the fact that the model is constructed out of two building
                         blocks: PPP and the balance of supply and demand in the money market. Not sur-
                         prisingly, given the failure of PPP to fit the facts, the monetary model also fares
                         rather poorly in that respect.
                            By way of contrast, the Mundell–Fleming model (Chapter 6) goes to the opposite
                         extreme of taking the price level as constant. Since it also ignores the role of
                         expectations its relevance to contemporary currency markets is limited, although
                         it has been very influential, both on academic researchers and on the architects of
                         macroeconomic policy, particularly in the UK and USA.
                            The Dornbusch model (Chapter 7) represents a compromise, suspending PPP in
                         the short run but acknowledging it as undeniable in the long run. The implication
                         turns out to be that financial markets, which are still assumed to clear instantane-
                         ously, have to overadjust to disturbances.
                            In fact, this conclusion is quite general, as was seen in the next two chapters. In
                         particular, overshooting is a feature of portfolio balance models (Chapter 8) in which
                         investors are seen as allocating their wealth to three broad asset categories: domestic
                         money and bonds and foreign currency bonds. It is also an implication of currency
                         substitution models (Chapter 9) in which investors are assumed to focus more
                         narrowly on the choice between domestic and foreign currency balances, shifting
                         their relative money demand in response to changes in the rate of depreciation.
                            Both models make strong predictions, especially with regard to the link between
                         the current account and the exchange rate. Neither fits the facts very closely and
                         neither proves reliable for forecasting purposes. The same criticism could be made of
                         the models outlined in Chapter 10, albeit for different reasons. In taking a general
                         equilibrium approach, the Redux model and its successors try to relate exchange
                         rate movements to the underlying structure of the economy and in particular to the
                         utility-maximizing choices of agents in each country. The aim is laudable, but the
                         outcome throws more light on international macroeconomics than on exchange
                         rate behaviour. Part II ends with a chapter on a topic in what is sometimes called
                         political economy: what does our understanding of exchange rates imply for the
                         optimal size of a currency zone? In particular, what are the likely effects of the new
                         European Monetary Union?
                            In Part III, the consequences of uncertainty, which had been avoided up to this
                         point, were confronted under three headings. Start with an equation like Equation
                         12.4, rewritten as follows:
                                                           st = ρt−1 + f t−1
                                                                         t
                                                                             + ut                         (18.1)
                            Chapter 12 looked at the role of the forward rate in this equation and in the
                         process introduced the important concepts of rational expectations and market
                         efficiency. Chapter 13 concentrated on the innovation term, ut, and showed that
                         it ought to be explained by the intermittent arrival of new information – ‘news’ –
                         about the fundamentals. In the next chapter, the risk premium, ρt−1 was linked to
                         the behaviour of individual decision makers faced with investment choices under
                         conditions of uncertainty.
ERA_C18.qxd 09/27/2004 03:09PM Page 477




                                                                           18.2 Where do we go from here?     477

                             Examination of the evidence revealed something of a puzzle. On the one hand,
                          unbiasedness could be ruled out with some confidence. In other words, the intercept
                          term in Equation 18.1 was not zero. On the other hand, from several points of view,
                          it was hard to credit that the risk premium could explain the gap between the spot
                          and lagged forward rate. The same applied to ‘news’: the theory contributed to some
                          extent to an explanation of the facts, but nowhere near enough.
                             Chapter 15 pointed to a possible reconciliation of some of the recurrent themes
                          in the book. It was shown there that in some cases non-linear models can generate
                          predictions for exchange rate behaviour that cover almost every variety of conceiv-
                          able pattern, ranging from almost mechanical cycles to fluctuations that are virtually
                          indistinguishable from randomness. It remains to be seen whether this type of model
                          will ultimately advance our understanding of how currency markets work.
                             Finally, Chapters 16 and 17 dealt with two aspects of fixed exchange rate regimes
                          that have been extensively analysed in the literature of the last few years. Target
                          zones are for all practical purposes a necessary concomitant of any fixed exchange
                          rate regime. Following through their implications yielded theoretical predictions that
                          were not quite what might have been expected in advance. The last chapter examined
                          the way fixed exchange rate systems break down once they have lost their credibility.
                          Again, the mechanism involves subtleties that might not have been obvious at first,
                          notably the fact that a fixed rate can be shown to fail precisely at the point where its
                          collapse results in no perceptible change.


                   18.2 Where do we go from here?
                          The reader may feel slightly cheated at the end of a book like this. After all, we do
                          not seem to know very much about exchange rates, do we? Or, more precisely, there
                          are lots of negative statements we can make with confidence: PPP does not explain
                          exchange rate fluctuations, neither do money stocks, nor interest rate differentials
                          . . . and so on.
                              In the first place it should be pointed out that negative results may still be worth
                          having.1 Sometimes, a process of elimination is the best one can do.
                              More than that, however, it has been made clear throughout the book that a
                          major reason why most theories of exchange rate determination fail is because of
                          their inability to explain the volatility we actually observe. Most of the candidate
                          variables proposed by the different theories are simply far too stable to fit the bill.
                              Now volatility is a general feature of financial markets. In fact, the currency mar-
                          kets can appear positively tranquil by comparison with some of the more turbulent
                          markets, such as stock markets for example.
                              Perhaps the very fact that turbulence is so widespread in financial markets is a clue
                          to how we ought to think about the problem. Suppose the factors that generate the
                          turbulence have causes which are common to financial markets, but which are com-
                          pletely independent of events in any specific market. In other words, suppose that
                          exchange rate volatility contains two components: one attributable simply to the
                          fact that currency markets behave like the financial markets of which they are an
                          example and another component reflecting fluctuations in the fundamentals.
                              Notice that this is not quite the same as what was called the ‘news’ approach in
                          Chapter 13. Fluctuations due to ‘news’ are, by definition, the result of the behaviour
ERA_C18.qxd 09/27/2004 03:09PM Page 478




         478 Chapter 18 · Conclusions

                         of investors with rational expectations operating in an efficient market. Instead, what
                         is being suggested here is that an underlying relationship between the fundamentals
                         and the exchange rate – perhaps along the lines of one of the models covered in the
                         first half of this book – may be swamped in practice by not one but two types of
                         turbulence: the volatility that characterizes financial markets in general super-
                         imposed on the volatility that results from the impact of ‘news’. Let us call the first
                         type: market volatility and the second: information volatility.
                             Now, if there were a way of stripping out the market volatility from our observed
                         exchange rate series, we would then be able to identify the appropriate fundamental
                         model by fitting a ‘news’ model to deal with the information volatility. Unfortun-
                         ately, we are as yet a long way from being able to explain market behaviour, although
                         an increasing amount of work has been published in recent years and the pace has
                         accelerated in the aftermath of the 1987 stock market crashes.
                             It should be appreciated in this regard that the problem of explaining stock
                         market volatility is subtly different from the problem of explaining exchange rate
                         volatility. To see why, take the case of a share in a company whose future profits
                         (and dividends) are known with certainty.2 Ask yourself what ‘model’ one would use
                         to determine the share price.
                             Put in this fashion the question has an obvious answer. We hardly need a model.
                         All we need do is capitalize the known future income stream. Furthermore, we have
                         proof that this present value model is correct because there are plenty of riskless
                         securities available (we simply call them bonds rather than shares) and, sure enough,
                         their market price never deviates very far from their present value, once account is
                         taken of differences in tax treatment, detailed redemption provisions and so on.
                             Notice the contrast with the situation in exchange rate research. Since they know
                         the identity of the fundamental variables, stock market researchers can confidently
                         attribute deviations from this benchmark to the effects of uncertainty. This gives
                         them a head start over exchange rate researchers in dealing with the types of ques-
                         tion covered in Chapters 12 and 13 of this book. Thus, for example, their variance
                         bounds tests on share prices have to be regarded as more conclusive than those on
                         exchange rates.
                             It seems likely, therefore, that progress on the research agenda in stock markets is
                         going to be very important in affecting our thinking about exchange rates. We have
                         already encountered an example of this. The work on bubbles (see Section 13.5)
                         was a response to evidence of stock market inefficiency. As was pointed out, it is a
                         special approach, insofar as it takes market perversity for granted without trying to
                         explain it. But attempts to explain market behaviour are being made. A number of
                         avenues are currently being explored:

                         (1) Alternatives to rational expectations: as we have seen, the direct (or survey-based)
                             evidence on RE is mixed. Work by Kahneman and Tversky (1979 and 1982) has
                             suggested a number of alternatives, often summarized under the heading of
                             behavioural finance, although its applicability to financial markets is yet to be
                             conclusively demonstrated.
                         (2) Market inefficiency: notably, recent work on so-called ‘noise trading’ in stock
                             markets (Black, 1988; Kyle, 1985). This research is very much in its infancy and
                             in any case it is not clear that it will produce any conclusions directly applicable
ERA_C18.qxd 09/27/2004 03:09PM Page 479




                                                                           18.2 Where do we go from here?     479

                              to currency markets. At best, it looks at the present moment as though it may
                              serve to provide a measure of theoretical rationalization for the type of models
                              being generated by the time-series theorists, whether stochastic or deterministic.
                          (3) Microstructural approach: in recent years, a number of researchers have followed
                              an approach almost the opposite of that taken in the Redux model. Instead of
                              broadening the focus of exchange rate determination, they narrow the focus,
                              concentrating instead on the fine detail of how currency markets work and how
                              the different types of agents interact (see Lyons, 2001).
                          (4) Non-linear time series (that is, stochastic models) may offer some hope of
                              describing, if not really explaining exchange rate movements. One reason for
                              turning in this direction (apart from the fact that the possibilities of linear time
                              series seem to have been exhausted) is to be found in an examination of high-
                              frequency data: weekly, daily or minute by minute. Two features are found to
                              emerge. First, the variance of exchange rate changes is plainly non-constant
                              itself. Second, the market seems to be characterized by relatively long periods of
                              tranquillity, punctuated by spells of turbulence.
                                 Chapter 15 looked at one approach to modelling this type of behaviour.
                              Another approach, so-called ARCH models and their variants, involves extend-
                              ing standard econometric or time-series models to incorporate a non-constant
                              error variance term. Usually, this involves a sub-model of the residual variance,
                              which is itself essentially a univariate time series (typically an ARMA(1,1) pro-
                              cess). The implication is that episodes of volatility tend to cluster, as a result of
                              spillovers from previous periods. To a great extent, this sort of process seems
                              to represent the facts about exchange rates quite well. Nonetheless, it clearly
                              does little to advance our understanding of why exchange rates fluctuate.
                              Nonlinearity of the kind covered in Section 2.6.2 has the attraction of being
                              more easily interpreted and looks at this stage to hold out some hope for the
                              future.
                             In the conclusion to the third edition of this book, I warned that the consequences
                          for exchange rates of globalization and in particular of electronic trading in goods,
                          services and securities were impossible to predict. It is still too soon to summarize the
                          overall impact of these developments, which, although rapid, must have much fur-
                          ther to go. However, I remain convinced that the erosion of political and economic
                          sovereignty implied by the new technologies will at some stage (possibly quite soon)
                          start to weaken the link between currencies and nationalities. In some respects, this
                          is already occurring, often for reasons that have nothing directly to do with global-
                          ization or technology. In addition to the obvious example of European Monetary
                          Union, there is also the beginning of what could be a trend towards currency boards.
                          But as usual a more powerful influence is likely to come from spontaneous market
                          forces. In general, the phenomenon called currency substitution in Chapter 9 is likely
                          to become far more widespread in the future, simply because the institutional and
                          political constraints which in the past prevented its becoming a practical reality are
                          quickly disappearing. For example, it is far easier today than it was even five years
                          ago to hold deposits in foreign currencies or indeed a number of different currencies,
                          switching at will between the two. It is increasingly difficult to pin a national flag on
                          the banks that offer these facilities to corporates and individuals – they are not only
ERA_C18.qxd 09/27/2004 03:09PM Page 480




         480 Chapter 18 · Conclusions

                         multinational in the accepted sense of having subsidiaries in a number of countries,
                         they are increasingly located nowadays in cyberspace, offering services which are
                         either internet based or phone based, with customers calling on local numbers
                         in, say, Glasgow, being routed seamlessly to call centres in India or Malaysia. Once
                         banks no longer have a home country, they no longer have a home currency. Their
                         large corporate customers have for some time been in the same situation, often list-
                         ing their shares on more than one major stock market and presenting their annual
                         accounts in two or more currencies.
                             By this stage, it is only the individual household consumer who stands in the way
                         of currency competition and he or she is likely to prove a very low hurdle indeed for
                         a number of reasons. First, and most important, the decision about the vehicle curr-
                         ency for transactions is often taken out of the hands of the consumer, who only sees
                         (and only cares about) the currency in which the transaction is invoiced. Second,
                         even where the consumer has a choice, the vehicle currency decision is often tied to
                         other more important decisions. When I am choosing between two internet offers on
                         my motor insurance, a foreign holiday or a bundle of CDs, whether the quote is in
                         dollars, pounds or euros is likely to be a minor consideration. The payment mech-
                         anism is the same in any case: an ordinary credit card makes it possible to convert
                         funds painlessly (and at money centre exchange rates) into even the most obscure
                         currencies.
                             Money evolved before the nation state and, in one form or another, it will outlive
                         it. Originally, money was either privately issued, by bankers of good standing in their
                         own right, or by kings or potentates whose nationality in the sense we understand the
                         term today was more or less undefined, but who were nonetheless able to enjoy the
                         benefits of seigniorage. Most ‘countries’ – kingdoms, dukedoms, principalities etc. –
                         never attempted to issue their own money, making payments instead either in gold
                         or whatever was the most commonly used local currency. Hence, currencies such as
                         the Thaler (from which, incidentally, we get the word dollar) became widely used
                         across western Europe by people who neither knew nor cared about its national
                         provenance, but were concerned only with its acceptability. It may well be that the
                         21st century will see a return to a high-tech version of that world. To some extent, it
                         is already foreshadowed in the constraints global currency markets are imposing on
                         national governments. Countries are being forced as never before to compete for the
                         favours of money holders. In terms of the Keynesian taxonomy of motives for hold-
                         ing money, while the speculative and precautionary demands have always been to a
                         greater or lesser degree sensitive to international competitive pressures, technology
                         has brought monetary competition into the transactions demand too.
                             The net effect of all these developments on exchange rates is difficult to foresee,
                         except insofar as it threatens to make the already feeble link between national income
                         and the value of a currency via the transactions demand for money completely invis-
                         ible. In the meantime, humility seems to be required. The final paragraph of the first
                         and second editions of this book ran as follows:
                            Perhaps the worst thing we could do would be to pretend that we know more than we
                            actually do – an affliction which seems to affect academics occasionally and politicians,
                            professional and amateur, very frequently – as witnessed by some of the arguments used in
                            Britain to support the case for EMS membership.
ERA_C18.qxd 09/27/2004 03:09PM Page 481




                                                                                                                  Notes    481

                          Those words were written in 1988. The history of Britain’s brief membership of EMS
                          illustrated the point perfectly: politicians and many economists held out the promise
                          in particular of lower interest rates to a gullible public. The outcome was, of course,
                          the complete opposite. The indictment is hubris: getting the forecast wrong is, alas,
                          one of the accepted perils of the trade, but the confidence with which the forecasts
                          were sold in the first place was less forgivable. Some of the advocates of EMU are in
                          this respect recidivists.
                              You have been warned.
